results.summary: This design performs nearest neighbor interpolation demosaicing for RGGB Bayer color filter arrays. It receives pixel data over a UART serial interface and outputs the demosaiced result over UART. The project is implemented in Verilog and fits in a single Tiny Tapeout tile. The documentation is minimal, providing only the title, one-line description, and pin names, so details of the implementation and testing are not available.

This project implements a simple I2C master controller that transmits one byte to a fixed slave address (0x50). It generates START and STOP conditions and provides BUSY, DONE, and ACK status outputs. The controller is controlled by an 8-bit data input and a START signal, and it drives the SDA and SCL lines. Testing requires an I2C slave device, logic analyzer, or oscilloscope to observe the signals.

This design implements the LEA-128 block cipher using an iterative approach. It loads a 128-bit key and data block serially through an input handshake protocol, then performs encryption or decryption based on control signals, and outputs the result serially through an output handshake. The design is implemented in Verilog and occupies a 2x2 tile area. Testing uses a test vector sourced from Wikipedia, but no external hardware is mentioned.

This design checks whether an 8-bit input value is a Fibonacci number. It compares the input against the Fibonacci numbers that fit in 8 bits and sets an output high if a match is found. The design is purely combinational and requires no external hardware. It is tested with a cocotb testbench that applies known Fibonacci and non-Fibonacci values.

This project computes the sine and cosine of an 8-bit input angle using an iterative 8-stage CORDIC algorithm in Q2.6 fixed-point format. The angle is provided on the input pins, and a start signal triggers the computation, with results available after about 11 clock cycles. The design is tested with a cocotb testbench that sweeps all 128 angles and checks against a golden model. External hardware is not required, but an optional 8-bit LED PMOD can be connected to view the cosine output.

This design implements a true random number generator using a ring oscillator as the entropy source. The oscillating signal is sampled by a clock, and the sampled bits are checked by a health checker to detect repeated patterns. Post-processing improves randomness and generates the final random output bits. The project is tested in simulation using Icarus Verilog and GTKWave, but no silicon test results are provided.

This design implements an adaptive neural spike detector with an IIR bandpass filter (300-3000 Hz), a nonlinear energy operator (NEO), and an EWMA adaptive threshold. It processes 8-bit signed ADC samples and outputs a spike detection pulse along with a 7-bit timestamp. The threshold multiplier and refractory period are configurable via a 3-wire SPI interface. The design is intended as a digital backend for neural recording AFEs and is tested with a cocotb testbench; external hardware such as an ADC or microcontroller is recommended for real-world use.

This project implements a 4-neuron spiking neural network using the Leaky Integrate-and-Fire model. Each neuron integrates input current, leaks a fraction of its membrane potential, and fires a spike when the threshold is reached. The weight matrix is programmed serially via a shift register, and spike outputs are provided for each neuron. The design is tested by programming weights and observing spike outputs; no external hardware is required.

This design is a hardware entropy mixing circuit that generates randomized outputs using XOR feedback paths. It accepts an 8-bit entropy input and produces an 8-bit randomized output stream. The design is lightweight and requires no external hardware. However, the documentation is very thin, providing only a high-level description and no details on testing or implementation.

This project is a simple implementation of the classic video game Pong. It generates a VGA video signal through the Tiny VGA Pmod and accepts input from a Gamepad Pmod, allowing two players to control paddles. The design was developed and verified on the Analogue Pocket and in the VGA Playground, with testing done visually rather than with an automated testbench. External hardware required includes a Gamepad Pmod and a Tiny VGA Pmod.
